messages.subject: parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
I'm trying to do the example 9.7.2 of BUGS book which includes that parameter constraint is a^2 + b^2 > 1. So I tried the following Stan code, but it didn't work.

parameters {
  real a;
  real b;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=1> theta;
  theta <- square(a) + square(b);
}

model {
  a ~ normal(0, 1);
  b ~ normal(0, 1);
}

Then, I used polar coordinate as follows, it seemed to work.

parameters {
  real<lower=1> r;
  real<lower=0, upper=2*pi()> theta;
}

transformed parameters {
  real a;
  real b;
  a <- r*cos(theta);
  b <- r*sin(theta);
}

model {
  a ~ normal(0, 1);
  b ~ normal(0, 1);
}

But, it says the following warning message when compiling. Do I have to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform? Please give me any advice.

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
  Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
    a ~ normal_log(...)
Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
  Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
    b ~ normal_log(...)

-Bee

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
Hi, I think the difficulty here is that you’re trying to define a truncated distribution by the back door, as it were.  In this case there are no parameters in your distribution (the means and variances are fixed at 0 and 1), so the normalizing factor in the truncation is a constant and can be ignored.  But if you replaced 0,1 in your model by parameters, you’d kinda be in trouble.  I don’t have the Bugs book handy so I don’t know why you want to constrain a^2 + b^2 to be greater than 1.  A simple option would be to run this unconstrained and than, at the end, discard all simulations in which a^2 + b^2 < 1.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
I'm used to seeing constraints where a^2 + b^2 < 1 to constrain
autoregressive models to stationarity. I don't think we can
handle the > 1 case easily, because it winds up being equivalent to

b > 1 or sqrt(a) > sqrt(1 - b^2)

which is equivalent to abs(a) > 1 - b^2, which we can't represent.

Andrew's suggestion is a kind of rejection sampling, which is only
going to be efficient if there aren't many simulations in which
a^2 + b^2 < 1. But then if there are simulatiosn where the constraint's
violated, then it typically says the data aren't consistent with the
constraint.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
On Wednesday, June 24, 2015 at 9:43:41 PM UTC-4, bee wrote:
But, it says the following warning message when compiling. Do I have to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform? Please give me any advice.

I think the polar coordinates parameterization would be the way to go in Stan for this toy model. According to

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box%E2%80%93Muller_transform

and under the constraint that R > 1, it would be

transformed data {
  real U;
  U <- exp(-0.5);
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0,upper=2*pi()> theta;
  real<lower=0,upper=U> U1;
}
model {
  // implicit uniform on theta and U1
}
generated quantities {
  real R;
  real a;
  real b;
  R <- sqrt(-2 * log(U1));
  a <- R * cos(theta);
  b <- R * sin(theta);
}

Of course, you could just do independent sampling in R

SIMS <- 10^6
U1 <- runif(SIMS, max = exp(-0.5))
theta <- runif(SIMS, max = 2 * pi)
R <- sqrt(-2 * log(U1))
a <- R * cos(theta)
b <- R * sin(theta)
smoothScatter(a,b,nrpoints=0)

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 1:53:04 AM UTC-4, bee wrote:
This code adds negative infinity to log posterior when constraint violates. I'm just wondering what differences are...

The differences are more fundamental than this particular toy example. BUGS is (primarily) a Gibbs sampler that draws from the full-conditional distribution of each parameter given all the other parameters. That BUGS code is sufficient to characterize the distributions of a | b and b | a.

The default algorithm in Stan is a lot more complicated but entails a mechanism to generate proposals for the joint distribution of the parameters a and b. So, you have to be able to express something proportional to the joint posterior density. If your prior density does not integrate to 1 over the parameter space because there is some hole in the middle, then you generally don't have something proportional to the joint posterior density. In your case, I think the hole has a constant size so it is actually proportional to a joint posterior density.

But the complicated mechanism to generate proposals for the joint distribution will not work well because it will often leapfrog through the high density region just outside the hole and land in the hole. It works much better when the parameter space is differentiable everywhere. Mike did a Stan example like this BUGS one starting at about 1 hour and 12 minutes in

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHsuIaPbNbY

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
Actually that example didn’t have any hard constraint, so there wasn’t any real hole.

The problem with a hole like this is that it changes the shape of parameter space
and Stan can’t handle that directly (formally for the math junkies — you’re trying to
sample from a distribution defined on R^{2} / D, with D a disc centered at zero, where 
as Stan can sample from only R^{n}).  The easiest thing to do is reject sample as
Andrew suggested.  There are two strategies for this.

Sample as usual and compute r = a^{2} + b^{2} in generated quantities.  Then take
your Stan output and remove any samples with r < 1.

Add a reject statement to your model black,

model {
  …
  if (a^{2} + b^{2} < 1)
    reject();
  ...
}

which will immediately throw the current sample away.

As Bob notes this can be inefficient if most of your posterior mass is near the disk
but there aren’t many other options given the wacky topology of this space.

Oh, and changing to polar coordinates won’t work!  We’ve talked about this before,
but the ultimately problem is that the Jacobian you need to add is an infinite sum
that can’t be computed in closed form.  Reparameterizations only work when you’re
mapping between spaces with the same shape (topology)!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
parts:
On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 8:59:31 PM UTC-4, bee wrote:
As Ben mentioned, I understand increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()) does not always mean reject() from the joint probability viewpoint. But, when the hole has a constant size like this case, can I replace reject() with increment_log_prob(negative_infinity())?

Both reject("in hole") and increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()) will result in the proposal being rejected. In principle, using reject("in hole") is a bit more efficient because it abandons the proposal immediately whereas doing increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()) will keep evaluating subsequent sampling statements that add or subtract to negative . But in practice, doing reject("in hole") spews so many informational messages that it takes a long time just to stream them to the screen.

But something like

parameters {
  real a;
  real b;
}
model {

if ( (square(a) + square(b)) < 1 ) reject("in hole")
  a ~ normal(0,1);
  b ~ normal(0,1);
}

achieves horrible efficiency and over half the transitions diverge

> summary(do.call(rbind, args = get_sampler_params(doughnut2, inc_warmup = FALSE)))
accept_stat__      stepsize__       treedepth__     n_leapfrog__    n_divergent__

Min.   :0.0000   Min.   :0.01162   Min.   :1.000   Min.   :  1.00   Min.   :0.0000
 1st Qu.:0.7991   1st Qu.:0.08288   1st Qu.:3.000   1st Qu.:  4.00   1st Qu.:0.0000
 Median :0.9737   Median :0.15227   Median :3.000   Median :  7.00   Median :1.0000

 3rd Qu.:0.9993   3rd Qu.:0.17738   3rd Qu.:4.000   3rd Qu.: 15.00   3rd Qu.:1.0000
 Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :0.19539   Max.   :8.000   Max.   :255.00   Max.   :1.0000


for a model where the Box-Mueller approach achieves terrific efficiency, no divergent transitions, and the same bivariate posterior distribution of a and b.

So don't rely on reject(), increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()), or inequality constraints on transformed parameters to do anything other than check for programmer mistakes or numerical over/underflow. Reparameterize your model so that there is a 1-to-1 mapping between some dense subset of the real numbers and the quantities of interest in your model.

Ben
